title: Which point / table / region satisfies it
subtitle: Linear inequalities in one or two variables · 19 official questions

sections.heading: Where this sits for you
body: **19 of the official questions in Linear inequalities in one or two variables are this one** — 3 Easy, 10 Medium, 6 Hard.
It is top-heavy: most versions are Hard, so it only earns study time once your target actually requires that tier.

sections.heading: How to spot it
body: You are looking at this pattern when:
- An inequality or a small system of inequalities is given.
- The choices are ordered pairs, three-row x–y tables, candidate values for one coordinate, or described regions such as quadrants and axes.
- The question asks which one is a solution, contains no solutions, or 'could be the value'.

sections.heading: The method
body: - 1) For tables or pairs, substitute the first x value into the inequality to get a bound on y.
- That usually eliminates three choices at once, and you confirm the survivor on the other rows.
- 2) For a point with one unknown coordinate in a system, substitute the known coordinate into each inequality and intersect the resulting bounds.
- 3) For regions, rewrite the inequality as y > … and check the sign of each term in that quadrant.
- If every term forces the wrong sign, the region has no solutions.

sections.heading: Where Desmos fits
body: Very fast.
Type the inequality or inequalities and plot the table points (use a table in Desmos) or the candidate pairs.
The one whose points all fall in the shaded, overlapping region is correct.
For regions, look at which quadrant the shading never reaches.

sections.heading: What it is built to catch
body: You check only one row of a table, or only one inequality of a system.
You treat a boundary point as a solution when the inequality is strict.
Or you forget to flip the sign when you divide by a negative coefficient while isolating y.

sections.heading: You are losing these
body: Before you choose, say out loud what the question is asking for — not what you solved for.
You check only one row of a table, or only one inequality of a system.
You treat a boundary point as a solution when the inequality is strict.
